A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NeRAF and retain the same core radiance-field, voxel-grid and acoustic-field framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original SoundSpaces RIR predictions, cross-modal image-synthesis results, few-shot experiments, grid and loss ablations, and inference measurements.

after.justification: v2 reports original SoundSpaces results and adds RAF and RWAVS experiments, including acoustic predictions, real-scene visual results and additional controlled analyses.

M1.justification: The core pipeline remains, but v2 replaces positional direction encoding with spherical harmonics and introduces NeRAF++ with an energy-decay loss and full-STFT training. Appendix A adds a monaural, source-direction-conditioned RAF configuration. Appendix J adapts NeRAF to query frequencies, predict STFT masks and use magnitude-STFT MSE for RWAVS. These substantially extend the documented procedures.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates six simulated indoor SoundSpaces scenes. v2 retains these and adds RAF's two real rooms with monaural RIRs and directional sources, plus recorded-audio synthesis on RWAVS Office, House, Apartment and Outdoors scenes. Appendix J also evaluates visual synthesis in real scenes.

E2.justification: SoundSpaces Table 1 adds NACF and NACF w/T to the retained AAC/Opus, NAF, INRAS and AV-NeRF comparators. The new RAF comparison includes energy-decay-trained NAF++ and INRAS++ alongside NACF variants. RWAVS Table A2 additionally evaluates ViGAS. Nerfacto remains the visual comparator.

E3.justification: v2 introduces RAF's 80/20 audio split, 0.32-second recordings, 48-kHz processing and camera subsampling, plus RWAVS MAG/ENV evaluation and sparse-image protocols. Within SoundSpaces, feature dimensions become scene-dependent, time normalization changes from [-1,1] to [0,1], and loss ablations expand from three to six scenes. Grid ablations and runtime measurement move to RAF. The main SoundSpaces 90/10 split and audio preprocessing remain.

E4.justification: v2 Table 3 adds a zero-filled-grid control that preserves the feature extractor, directly testing scene information beyond parameter count. It replaces the SoundSpaces grid study with a RAF study and expands the loss analysis. RAF few-shot curves, loudness-map visualizations and RWAVS cross-modal visual analyses add substantial evidence about data efficiency and model behavior.

E5.justification: v1 does not specify repeated-run counts. v2 Section 4.2 newly reports six repetitions per experiment and averaging; this does not establish an increase over v1's unspecified count. Neither version supplies seed identities, dispersion estimates, confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: SoundSpaces Table 1 revises NeRAF's T60/C50/EDT errors from 2.04%/0.39 dB/0.011 s to 2.14%/0.38 dB/0.010 s alongside configuration changes. Vision scores, few-shot curves and ablation results also change. Extensive RAF and RWAVS results are added. RWAVS Table A2 reports mixed rankings: NeRAF's overall ENV is lower than AV-NeRF's, 0.144 versus 0.145, while MAG is higher, 1.596 versus 1.504.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix C adds the formal energy-decay objective through per-window energy, reverse cumulative energy and a log-space L1 discrepancy, following cited prior work (Equations 11-14). This is a limited addition to the mathematical loss formulation. No new theorems, proofs or theoretical guarantees are introduced.

C1.justification: The central claims about 3D scene conditioning, independent modality rendering and beneficial cross-modal learning remain. The abstract and introduction broaden stated validation to RAF. v1's prominent claim of outperforming prior work with half the audio data is no longer retained; v2's replacement few-shot statement requires 75% of the data for superiority across all metrics.

C2.justification: v2 reinterprets grid benefits using the capacity-preserving zero-grid control and explicitly presents loss selection as a T60-versus-C50/EDT tradeoff. It removes the lack-of-real-data limitation and adds distinctions between recorded-audio fitting and reusable RIR prediction, plus a grid-detail explanation for RWAVS House underperformance. v1's explicit single-source and difficult-RIR-acquisition limitations are omitted; scene-specific training and static-scene limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 documents NeRAF++ loss weights and batches of 34 complete STFTs, monaural output configuration, RAF camera selection and preprocessing, and RWAVS-specific settings. It newly specifies pose normalization with a 1 mm margin and the waveform-to-STFT evaluation procedure. Feature-size assignments conflict between Appendices B and F. v1's license-information table is removed, while the project-page reference remains.

R1.justification: v2 adds NACF discussion, distinguishing NeRAF's scene priors from NACF's assumed surface acoustic coefficients. It also adds RAF and VR-NeRF references and a ViGAS citation for the new evaluations. The broader related-work organization and positioning remain largely intact.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction and method explanations, replaces the contribution bullet list with prose, and removes the separate Task section. It reorganizes the appendices and moves societal impact out of the main discussion. These changes substantially revise the narrative independently of the added experiments.

P2.justification: Figures 1-4 are redrawn, and visual comparisons gain larger panels and highlighted artifacts. Table 1 combines SoundSpaces and RAF comparisons; Table 2 expands from averaged deltas to per-scene absolute scores and deltas. New loudness maps, RAF few-shot plots and RWAVS tables accompany extensive rearrangement of appendix displays and a changed document template.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly lacked real-world validation, an important gap for its intended applications. v2 addresses this with RAF RIR experiments and RWAVS audio/vision results, while stronger comparators and the zero-grid control better test its central claims. Explicit loss tradeoffs and mixed RWAVS outcomes improve the assessment of applicability. Missing uncertainty estimates, inconsistent feature assignments and removed license information remain weaknesses, but the gains in empirical relevance and experimental control are substantial.
